speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, it supports the revision of all Acts on our Statute Book.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I will give an overview of each of these aspects and touch on the key amendments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The present Revised Edition of the Acts of Singapore was published almost 35 years ago in 1987.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Since then, many new Acts have been enacted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Many existing Acts have been extensively amended as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Just looking at the past decade, from 2011 to 2015, 160 Bills were introduced in Parliament, of which 111 were amendment Bills.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: From 2015 to 2020, 225 Bills were introduced, of which 161 were amendment Bills.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The length of each of the Bill has also increased over time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This increase in legislation reflects the increasing complexity and also the scope of coverage of legislation, and its role in governance of this country.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, as the Singapore Statute Book grows in size, it is even more important that our laws remain easy to understand, accessible and navigable by the public.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Since 2014, our law drafters have consciously used plain English drafting techniques for new legislation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The aim is to make the language of the law as modern, easy to understand and as simple as possible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is the Plain Laws Understandable by Singaporeans initiative or PLUS, which sprang from public feedback in to AGC’s Legislation Division on how legislation is drafted and presented.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some examples of plain English drafting techniques, which I am sure Members would appreciate, are as follows.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The length of each legislative sentence has been shortened, with long sentences and provisions broken up into different paragraphs or sub-paragraphs for easy navigation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Archaic words like "hereinafter", "hereby", and so on, which lawyers sometimes use all too often, are no longer used, as far as possible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Gendered expressions are replaced with gender-neutral expressions, so "Chairperson" instead of "Chairman", and so on.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For existing legislation, the Revised Edition of the Laws Act provides for them to be revised to be more user-friendly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Law revision is carried out by the Law Revision Commissioners, with the support of AGC’s Legislation Division.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In preparing a revised edition, the Commissioners can modernise and simplify the language of an Act or subsidiary legislation, provided that they do not change the meaning.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, for example, lengthy phrases and big words are replaced by simpler ones in the manner which I have outlined earlier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As far as possible, "shall" is replaced with "must" to signify legal obligation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Commissioners also consolidate an Act with all subsequent amendments, so that the amended Act can be read as one unified document.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Commissioners can also supply additional material that are useful to legislation users, such as information about the commencement date of each legislative provision.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is a huge undertaking that started in August 2017 and will be the first universal revision since the 1985 Edition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will be the ninth exercise that we have undertaken since Singapore had its own laws.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The 2020 Edition is estimated to contain about 510 Acts and 27,000 pages.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: By way of comparison, in 1985, that Edition comprised 387 Acts and about 8,000 pages.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I will take Members through some of the main clauses to illustrate the purport and intent of these amendments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 4 will give the Commissioners additional powers to make editorial changes to legislation to bring it in line with modern law drafting practice, but without changing the meaning.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will enable the Commissioners to introduce some of the modern drafting techniques that I have outlined earlier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 11(b) makes a related amendment to the Interpretation Act to emphasise that changes in drafting styles are not, in themselves, changes to the meaning of legislation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 5(b) and (c) will do away with the need to assign Chapter numbers to an Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These numbers provide limited information about the Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Sometimes, a Chapter number of a repealed Act is reused for a new Act, and this can sometimes lead to confusion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Acts in the new revised edition will, therefore, not have any Chapter numbers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 5(a) provides for all Acts in force as of 31 December 2020 to be included in the new revised edition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Legislation coming into force after that date can still be included at the discretion of the Commissioners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Commissioners intend to bring the entire revised edition into force on 1 July this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Commissioners also intend to use their existing powers to introduce two new features.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, the short titles of Acts will include their year of enactment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, the Penal Code will be cited as “Penal Code 1871”.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With the year of enactment, users will immediately have a rough idea of the history and how long ago such an Act was enacted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, each Act will also be supplemented with a complete and verified legislative history, tracing an Act’s history from its first enactment and through each subsequent amendment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will be helpful to lawyers, academics and students alike, and others who need to trace and understand the evolution of a particular provision in the Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Just as this House and its delegates make laws, the body of laws needs to be maintained to ensure that it is, and remains, accessible to all.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The amendments to the Revised Edition of the Laws Act demonstrate and underscore how much importance we place on the Rule of Law by striving towards ensuring that our laws are navigable, accessible and easily understood by the people of Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The universal revision exercise, as I have mentioned earlier started some years ago, has also led to the identification of various Acts and provisions that are obsolete.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Part 4 of the Bill seeks to repeal these obsolete laws.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 15 repeals spent or obsolete transitional provisions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These provisions were only intended to operate for a transitional period and are no longer necessary today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To give an example, Clause 15(1) repeals section 69(2) of the Accountants Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That provision allows the Minister to amend any written law which is inconsistent with the Accountants Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The intention of section 69(2) was to bridge any gap between existing laws and the newly enacted Accountants Act then, at that point in time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Any transitional amendments made by the Minister under section 69(2) would have been made closer to 2004 when the Accountants Act was enacted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Any further amendments to the Act are to be made in the ordinary way, through an Amendment Act passed in Parliament.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Indeed, this has been done several times since that Act was passed in 2004.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Hence, section 69(2) of the Accountants Act is no longer relevant today and can be repealed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 16 of the Bill repeals consequential provisions that were superseded by events and never commenced.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, Clause 16(1) repeals section 65 of the CareShield Life and Long-Term Care Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Section 65 of that Act makes consequential amendments to the Bankruptcy Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, that provision had not been commenced by the time the Bankruptcy Act was repealed by the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act which came into force in July 2020.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With the repeal of the Bankruptcy Act, section 65 of the CareShield Life and Long-Term Care Act has, therefore, been superseded and should be repealed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I now come to Clauses 17 to 26 of the Bill, which I am sure Members would have gone through.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It seeks to repeal obsolete Acts or obsolete parts of some Acts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some of these Acts were enacted many decades ago and are archaic and no longer applicable today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For Members' benefit, for example, Clause 26 repeals the Personal Injuries (Emergency Provisions) Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This Act was enacted in 1941 to establish a compensation scheme for war injuries sustained by workers or civil defence volunteers during World War II.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I think, by my description alone, one can appreciate why we seek to repeal that obsolete Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It has been 75 years since World War II ended.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They take similar a vein, as what I have illustrated.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But if Members have any specific questions on the provisions, I will be happy to address them in my reply later.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This deals with the delegation of ministerial functions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is common for Acts of Parliament to confer functions on Ministers, who are ultimately responsible to Parliament for the exercise of executive authority.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Prime Minister then assigns the responsibility for each Act to a Minister.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ministers, in turn, can delegate their functions under the current section 36 of the Interpretation Act with the President’s approval.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, the existing framework only allows for the delegation of functions “in the absence of any provision of law to the contrary”.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This restriction, therefore, depends on the context in which the specific enactment is made in the Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Even if there is no express restriction in the Act against delegation, an implied parliamentary intention or a common law rule could prevent a delegation when it was not intended.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The uncertainty as to whether a function may or may not be delegated is at odds with a rule that is meant to make public administration more efficient.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If a function is non-delegable, the Minister cannot delegate it at all, not even to a Second Minister in the same Ministry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The first tier provides for delegations by the responsible Minister to a political officeholder in his or her Ministry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This could be a Second Minister, a Minister of State or a Parliamentary Secretary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These delegations require the Prime Minister’s approval because, constitutionally, the Prime Minister has the prerogative of assigning responsibilities to political officeholders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, because political officeholders are directly accountable to Parliament, the scope for delegation is also wider.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This would include statutory appeals that must currently be heard and decided by the Minister himself.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, function cannot be delegated if any Act expressly prohibits delegation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, the power to make subsidiary legislation, which is already delegated from the Legislature, cannot be further delegated.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, the power to delegate under this section cannot itself be delegated.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is not too different from the position that we have today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Delegation under the second tier of the framework is subject to any contrary legislative intention, which can be expressed or implied from the statutory context.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Whether there is a contrary intention is really a matter of statutory interpretation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Relevant factors will include the nature and gravity of the function, as well as considerations of administrative necessity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The three restrictions that I have mentioned earlier – the three classes – also apply to the second tier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One point to note though is that the scope for delegation under the second tier is not as broad as the first tier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is appropriate because the range of possible delegates under this second tier is wider.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Once a function is delegated under the new framework, the delegate will have the power to exercise the function in his or her own name.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With this two-tier delegation framework, statutory functions can be more effectively performed and, where appropriate, by delegates as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A delegation also does not prevent the responsible Minister from exercising the function.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In practice, the responsible Minister will continue to personally consider the most serious cases and exercise oversight over his or her delegates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members will recall that the Constitution was amended in May last year to enable Parliament to sit under continuity arrangements in times of exigency.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In such times, Article 64A enables Parliament to meet, with Members of Parliament spread out over two or more places appointed by the President.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Part 3 makes two amendments to the Parliament (Privileges, Immunities and Powers) Act in consequence of the constitutional amendments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This clarifies that the privileges, powers and immunities of Parliament and its Members extend to all places appointed by the President under those continuity arrangements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Any interference with such communication links can be disruptive to Parliamentary business.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will focus on the amendments on the delegation of ministerial functions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would be very useful to the Court to have clear guidance on how contrary intention should be inferred.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Court of Appeal in Asia Development Pte Ltd vs Attorney-General   SGCA 22 cited an English case for the position that the Court should consider the nature, scope and purpose of the function vested in the Minister and the relevant language of the statute and of the specific provision.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Moving forward, would the Ministry consider requiring Ministries to include more express language on the delegation of Ministerial function when drafting Bills to avoid Courts having to go through the process of inferring intention?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the Bill allows delegation of function to a public body or a public officer.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Helpfully, the Bill clarifies that if a ministerial function depends on the Minister’s opinion, belief or state of mind, the delegate may exercise the function based on the delegate’s opinion, belief or state of mind.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While this can be done where a ministerial function is delegated to a public officer, it is less clear how opinion, belief or state of mind of a public body should be determined.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, the Court of Appeal, again, in Asia Development Pte Ltd vs Attorney-General   SGCA 22, suggested that it is good practice for Government agencies to clearly identify the role and capacity in which they are acting, and to explain this promptly when challenged.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Court also noted that it would be helpful to adopt a measure of formality in communication of Government decisions so that there is little room for confusion over which party one is dealing with and in what capacity they are acting.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I just want to go into one clarification before I answer Mr Louis Ng's three questions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng cited Asia Development and raised some good points regarding the delegation of the Ministerial functions under the new section 36 of the Interpretation Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I just want to point out for this House that Asia Development deals with the devolution of Ministerial functions under the Carltona principle.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The principle is explained in the Explanatory Notes of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is a common law principle established by the English Court of Appeal case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In that case, the Court of Appeal recognised that a Minister's duties and powers are normally exercised by responsible officers who act under the authority of the Minister.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is also recognised that the decision of the officer is the decision of the Minister in this instance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the other hand, what is being introduced in this Bill is a delegation of Ministerial functions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Conceptually, delegation is quite different from a devolution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Where a power has been delegated under the Interpretation Act, which is what this Bill seeks to do, the delegate exercises the power in his or her own name, as I have explained in my speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In contrast, where a power is devolved under the Carltona principle, then the authorised officer exercises the power in the name of the Minister.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I just want to clarify that before I address Mr Louis Ng's three questions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Both delegation and devolution though are important tools to allow the Government to respond quickly and effectively to the needs of Singaporeans.There are also clear lines of accountability to Parliament, and to the public.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked how one might discern, the contrary intention as appears in the Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think the question is, what are the factors we look at to discern this contrary intention.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng would know that that is actually a matter of statutory construction and is not uncommon for pieces of legislation to contain this phrase "unless the contrary intention appears".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the Interpretation Act alone, the phrase appears more than 20 times.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, this is a concept that the Courts will be familiar with, legislative users are familiar with, and how to interpret them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the more specific question as to how this contrary intention against delegation can be inferred, there are well-established principles that can be applied.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The express language of the legislation should first be looked at.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is the best indication of what the intention of the draftsmen is in that piece of legislation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The intention can also be implied by statutory context, by looking at the overall architecture and context, the construction of the provisions and the location in which this particular provision sits in the context of the broader provisions in the Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked what other relevant factors could be taken into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These include the nature and gravity of a function, and I think Mr Louis Ng himself mentioned, the nature, purpose and scope – they are not different – as well as considerations of administrative necessity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked whether statutes can expressly address the question of delegation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think to the extent possible, this would be made clear in provisions and that is part of the exercise that the AGC is undertaking.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Specific provisions in an Act of Parliament may allow the delegation of functions, for instance, by providing that a Minister may authorise another person to exercise certain functions that are conferred on the Minister by that Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The new delegation framework in this Bill does not affect those statutory provisions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng's second question is how a public body's opinion, belief, or state of mind should be determined.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But at the same time, it is also made up of natural persons.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the natural persons will usually comprise a Chairperson or some other members within the body.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is also not uncommon for the Chief Executive to sit as a member of the public body.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The opinion of the public body would therefore be the opinion of the constituent persons, and this opinion would be formed in the same manner as how a public body ordinarily makes a decision.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, if a Statutory Board can make a decision by a simple majority of its members, then this simple majority can likewise form an opinion for the purposes of making that particular decision.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The exact process would, of course, depend on the legislation that constitutes the public body and any rules that they apply to the process under which the public body undertakes that decision-making.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think I have touched on all the questions that he has raised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With that, Madam, I beg to move.      .
